target_customer: Readers who pay a monthly subscription for ebooks, audiobooks and documents, plus uploaders who publish documents for free
problem: Publishing and sharing written work online was slow and fragmented. Adler cited his father's medical research taking 18 months to publish as the spark.
business_model: Started as ad supported document sharing; later freemium subscription (about $11.99 per month) with ads on the free tier
product_category: Digital reading library and document sharing

founders.name: Trip Adler
founders.background_notes: Came up with the idea at Harvard

founders.name: Jared Friedman
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as Founder and CTO; he later became a YC partner

founders.name: Tikhon Bernstam
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder by Wikipedia and PR Newswire

technical_complexity.rationale: Hosting, converting and rendering many document formats in the browser at scale (the iPaper Flash viewer) and indexing text for search was real engineering for a small team in 2007, but used standard components.

defensibility.rationale: User uploaded content and search traffic built a large corpus that later became the base of a licensed subscription library, but the initial upload product was copyable by rivals like Issuu and Docstoc.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent bought it. Scribd stayed independent and in 2020 bought SlideShare from LinkedIn.

market_need_then: Documents were hard to publish and discover on the web and no 'YouTube for documents' existed; TechCrunch's launch coverage in 2007 tagged Scribd with that label, showing early attention. Demand evidence beyond that was not retrieved.

branding.domain_note: Operates at scribd.com; no domain history found

identity.logo: Wordmark; a 2025 identity by Mother Design uses a wide bracketed sans wordmark with the name set in brackets
identity.voice_and_tone: Mission led: 'Real knowledge, uploaded by real people' on the site

branding.brand_signature: The YouTube for documents label at launch (given by TechCrunch)

rebrands.to: Scribd as company with separate product brands
rebrands.why: A design studio write-up says the original name stayed with the document business as the company split into separate products; date and exact detail from one source

branding.community_and_virality: Large user uploaded corpus, 300M+ documents claimed on its own site; no merch or fan culture found

brand_strength.rationale: Well known as a document site with broad search traffic and a paying subscriber base, but no iconic mascot or cultural presence found in sources.

pivots.from: Free document sharing with ad revenue
pivots.why: Date from background knowledge; not verified in this session's sources, the January 2015 PR names the book subscription service as the use of new funds

outcome_analysis: Scribd launched in March 2007 as a user upload document site, raised about $3.7M in June 2007 and $9M in December 2008, and led its category by 2009 with 12 million monthly visitors per TechCrunch. It later turned the corpus into a subscription library, took Khosla money in 2015 and $58M in 2019, bought SlideShare in 2020, and remains active with 300 staff. Success came from owning search traffic for documents, then pivoting to paid content.
notes: Series A conflict: StartupIntros says $4M with Andreessen Horowitz, other sources say $3.7M from Redpoint and Kinsey Hills; used the latter. Aggregator valuations (about $38M in 2009, $168M in 2015, $430M secondary) are single source and not recorded as rounds. Reported 2021 IPO plan at about $1B did not result in a listing in sources seen. Round labels are approximate. No competitor sources dated at the 2007 founding were retrieved (Docstoc, Issuu and SlideShare are named only in 2007 to 2009 era commentary), so the list is left empty. Pivot date is from background knowledge and unverified. Trinity Ventures was not found in sources.
